# Load the Data

movies <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2021/2021-03-09/movies.csv',

# Section 1: Linear Regression
Research Question: Among these movies, how does domestic gross revenue change with budget? Is that pattern different for movies that pass vs. fail the Bechdel test?

    # Part A:
Budget_2013 has 0 missing values. Domgross_2013 has 18 missing values.

```{r}
# Summary of Budget variable
summary(movies$budget_2013)
# mean = 55,464,608, median = 36,995,786
# mean is very far from median, let's check the distribution in a histogram and boxplot
ggplot(movies, aes(x = budget_2013)) + geom_histogram() 
ggplot(movies, aes(x = budget_2013)) + geom_boxplot()
# The distribution is skewed heavily to the right, shown by both the histogram and the boxplot. The boxplot is showing lots and lots of outliers.
```

```{r}
# Summary of Domestic Gross Revenue variable
summary(movies$domgross_2013)
# mean = 9.517e+07, median = 5.599e+07
# again, mean far from median. Highest grossing/budgeted movies must be skewing the distribution quite a bit
ggplot(movies, aes(x = domgross_2013)) + geom_histogram() 
ggplot(movies, aes(x = domgross_2013)) + geom_boxplot()
# skewed to the right, lots of outliers 
```

```{r}
# Quick look at Bechdel Test variable
# 0 missing values
table(movies$binary) 
# 803 pass, 991 fail
table(movies$clean_test)
```

```{r}
# Try log-transforming the budget2013 and domgross2013 data to see if the distribution becomes a little more balanced.
ggplot(movies, aes(x = log(budget_2013))) + geom_histogram()
ggplot(movies, aes(x = log(domgross_2013))) + geom_histogram()
# The log transformation makes the distributions look a little more Normal, though both variables still have some pretty extreme outliers. However, I think it is okay to proceed with making a model using the log-transformed data, I will just make sure to remain a little skeptical of the output/accuracy of the model.
```

Cleaning the Data: remove NAs 

```{r}
# Removing NAs from domgross_2013
movies <- movies %>% 
    filter(!is.na(domgross_2013)) 

# It is with this data that I will proceed with making a model for linear regression. Depending on the fit of the model as well as the diagnostic plots, I might repeat the modeling process after removing some extreme outliers to combat overfitting if that appears to be present.
```

Now that data is cleaned, let's make a model.

```{r}
# Linear regression model of the relationship between budget_2013 and domgross_2013, including the interaction of Bechdel test status (binary). 
linear_regression_model <- lm(log(domgross_2013) ~ log(budget_2013) * binary,
                            data = movies)
summary(linear_regression_model)

# Coefficients for this model are:
# log(budget_2013): 0.77898
# binaryPASS: -0.95063
# log(budget_2013):binaryPASS: 0.05204

# The first coefficient tells us that in groups that fail the Bechdel test, a 1% increase in budget is associated with a 0.779% increase in domestic gross revenue.

# Coefficient interaction term is 0.05204, meaning that the rate of change in domestic gross revenue as it is related to budget is 0.05% higher for movies that pass the Bechdel test than those that fail the test.

# The only p value that is significant in the output of this model is for log(budget_2013), suggesting budget might have a strong relationship with the outcome of domestic gross revenue. 
```

```{r}
# Plot of the relationship between budget_2013 and domgross_2013, with two fitted lines for the Bechdel test factors
ggplot(movies, 
        aes(x = log(budget_2013), y = log(domgross_2013), color = binary)) +
        geom_point() +
        geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

```{r}
# Run diagnostic plots for the model
dev.off()
par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(linear_regression_model)
```


What happens to the model when we remove the outliers from each variable?
```{r}
#outlier threshold for budget_2013
summary(movies$budget_2013)
78337905 + 1.5*(78337905 - 16068918) #171741386

#outlier threshold
summary(movies$domgross_2013)
1.217e+08 + 1.5*(1.217e+08 - 2.055e+07) #273425000

# clean the data again now, keeping data below these values
no_outliers <- movies %>% 
    filter(!is.na(domgross_2013), domgross_2013 < 273425000) %>%
    filter(budget_2013 < 171741386) %>%
    select(domgross_2013, budget_2013, binary)

summary(no_outliers)
ggplot(no_outliers, aes(x = log(domgross_2013))) + geom_histogram()
ggplot(no_outliers, aes(x = log(budget_2013))) + geom_histogram()
# Honestly, the distributions do not look that much different. Will make a model to see if the outputs change drastically (e.g., changes in significance of the variables)
```

```{r}
no_outlier_regression <- lm(log(domgross_2013) ~ log(budget_2013) * binary,
                            data = no_outliers)
summary(no_outlier_regression)

# Coefficients:
# log(budget_2013): 0.7521
# binaryPASS: -0.59209
# log(budget_2013): binaryPASS: 0.03619

ggplot(no_outliers, 
        aes(x = log(budget_2013), y = log(domgross_2013), color = binary)) +
        geom_point() +
        geom_smooth(method = "lm")

# The coefficients in this new model are not super different from the ones from the previous model. Also, the only variable that is suggested to be significant in the new model is budget_2013, which is the same as the first model. It was good to try and remove the outliers from the data for the model, but I think output suggests that the outliers are not affecting the model that much and that we can interpret the output from the first linear regression model. 
```

# Part B: Interpretation
1) The coefficient for budget, as a description of these movies is 0.77898. This means that given that a movie does not pass the Bechdel test, for every 1% increase in movie budget, domestic gross revenue is expected to increase 0.778%. The rate of change is in percentage because the model was created with log-transformed data. 
2) The coeffcient for the interaction term is 0.05204. This means that the rate of change in domestic gross revenue as it is related to budget is 0.05% higher for movies that pass the Bechdel test than those that fail the test.
3) The F-statistic generated from the model is associated with a pvalue of 2.2e-16, suggesting that at least one factor built into this model is producing a significant effect on the response variable, domestic gross revenue. From the model output we can see that this factor is likely budget, which has a larger standardized t value and a significant p value, while the interaction term and coefficient for binaryPASS alone are not significant in this model. Therefore I conclude that budget probably does have some kind of effect on domestic gross revenue (which lines up with what I generally know about the movie industry), but that whether a movie passes or fails the Bechdel test likely does not have a significant effect on domestic gross revenue.

# Part C: Diagnostic Plots 
Normality: The Q-Q plot shows us that a majority of the points lie on the line, which indicates normality. At the tails, the points do start to fall off the line, but because the majority in the center of the distribution lay flat on the line, there can be a reasonable assumption that the data has normality. 

Constant Variance: Looking at the Residuals vs. Fitted plot, the residuals seem to be generally randomly scattered around the 0 line, suggesting there is reason to assume the data has constant variance.

I think we can conclude that the model assumptions are reasonably met for this comparison. I would definitely still remain pretty skeptical of its overall fit and accuracy because there are a lot of extreme values. I also probably wouldn't use this model to predict gross revenue for new movies, but I think it can be helpful to describe the general trend/relationship between movie budget and revenue.



# Section 2: Logistic Regression

Research Question: What movie characteristics predict passing the Bechdel test?

# Part A: Model Fitting
fitting a logistic model that predicts Bechdel test oucome from budget_2013, year, and IMDB rating

```{r}
# Create a binary outcome (0/1) from the "binary" variable
movies$binary <- ifelse(movies$binary == "PASS", 1, 0)
# Add columms changing the units to per million dollars of budget, and change from year to decade
movies <- movies %>%
    mutate(budget_millions = budget_2013 / 1000000,
    decade = year / 10)

# Create a logistic regression model 
model <- glm(binary ~ budget_millions + decade + imdb_rating, data = movies, family = "binomial")
summary(model)
exp(coef(model)) # calculates the odds ratio
```

Coefficients (using millions of dollars as units and decade)
budget_millions: -0.0066, odds ratio: 0.9934
decade: 0.1786, oddds ratio: 1.1956
imdb rating: -0.2959, odds ratio: 0.7439


the log odds change by the Beta, whcih is the coefficients associated with each variable in the output
odds of outcome multiply by the odds ratio


```{r}
# create 95% confidence intervals
exp(confint(model))
confintervals_table <- tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) # exponentiate turns the log odds into the odds ratios for the table
```

```{r}
# Calculating Percent Change by Effect of Each Variable
print(paste("Percent change:", round((0.9934-1)*100, 2), "%")) # budget_millions 
print(paste("Percent change:", round((1.1956-1)*100, 2), "%")) # decade
print(paste("Percent change:", round((0.7439-1)*100, 2), "%")) # imdb rating
```

# Part B: Interpretation
For every $1 million increase in budget, the odds of a movie passing the Bechdel test decreases by 0.66%, which is a pretty negligible change and suggests budget does not have a significant effect on changing the odds of a movie passing or failing the Bechdel test. For every decade that passes, the odds of a movie passing the Bechdel test increases by 19.56%, which might suggest a significant effect. Lastly, for every 1-point increase in IMDB rating, the odds of a movie passing the Bechdel test decreases by 25.61%, which suggests an even stronger effect than release decade. According to this logistic regression, IMDB rating seems to have the strongest effect on the odds of a movie passing or failing the Bechdel test.

# Question 3: Comprehensive Analysis
Research Question: Among the movies in this dataset, does the relationship between budget and revenue look different across MPAA ratings?

```{r}
# Looking at "rated" variable
table(movies$rated)
# variable includes ratings such as NC-17, NR, TV-14, TV-PG, Unrated, and X. But we are only looking at G, PG, PG-13, and R. So we will drop all those others. There are also 207 NAs, we will drop those too. Dropping 207 NAs and 31 rows with other ratings.

# quick look at the distribution across factors of this variable
movies %>%
    filter(!is.na(rated)) %>%
    filter(rated %in% c("G", "PG", "PG-13", "R")) %>%
    ggplot(., aes(x = rated)) + geom_bar()

# Here we see that movies rated R and PG-13 have the highest frequency in this dataset.

# make subsetted data with NAs and other ratings removed, to use for linear regression model
movies_clean <- movies %>% 
    filter(!is.na(rated)) %>%
    filter(rated %in% c("G", "PG", "PG-13", "R"))

movies_clean$rated <- as.factor(movies_clean$rated)

# code to generate model, looking at relationship b/w budget and revenue, with an interaction of MPAA rating
model_budrevrating <- lm(log(domgross_2013) ~ log(budget_2013) * rated, data = movies_clean)
summary(model_budrevrating)

ggplot(movies_clean,
        aes(x = log(budget_2013), y = log(domgross_2013), color = rated)) +
            geom_point()+
            geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
            labs(x = "Log(Movie Budget) ($)", y = "Log(Domestic Gross Revenue) ($)", title = "Interaction of MPAA Ratings on the Relationship Between Movie Budget and Domestic Gross Revenue") +
            theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10)) +
            labs(caption = "Note: variables 2013-adjusted and log transformed")
# Model output summary tells us that at least one variable in this model has a significant effect on the relationship between budget and revenue. The Beta1 for log(budget_2013), given that the MPAA rating is G, shows that for every 1% increase in budget_2013, domgross_2013 increases by 0.57%. The p value associated with this is 0.015, suggesting significance. The other interaction levels do not seem to be significant. There is not enough evidence to suggest that changing the MPAA rating of a movie has any effect on the relationship between budget and domestic gross revenue.
```


```{r}
# Does the pattern change when we get rid of G rated movies?
movies_nog <- movies_clean %>%
      filter(rated %in% c("PG", "PG-13", "R"))

model_nog <- lm(log(domgross_2013) ~ log(budget_2013) * rated, data = movies_nog)
summary(model_nog)
ggplot(movies_nog,
        aes(x = log(budget_2013), y = log(domgross_2013), color = rated)) +
            geom_point()+
            geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
            labs(x = "Log(Movie Budget) ($)", y = "Log(Domestic Gross Revenue) ($)", title = "Interaction of MPAA Ratings on the Relationship Between Movie Budget and Domestic Gross Revenue") +
            theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10)) +
            labs(caption = "Note: variables 2013-adjusted and log transformed")
# This model output shows us something a lot different. The p-values associated with the effect of each of the interaction terms suggest that their effect on the relationship between budget and revenue is significant. This should make us doubt the stability of our first model, which had a vastly different conclusion.
par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_budrevrating)
plot(model_nog)
```

Findings
I used a linear regression model to examine the relationship between movie budget, domestic gross revenue, and the interaction of movies' MPAA ratings. The first model, which included G ratings along with PG, PG13, and R, suggested that changing the MPAA rating of the movie would not have a significant effect on the relationship that budget has to revenue. However, when we excluded the 36 G-rated movies from the dataset and created a second model, we got very different results. The model output showed us that changing the movie MPAA rating to any of the ratings (PG, PG13, R) posed a significant effect on the relationship between budget and revenue. This leads me to wonder about the stability of the model, and if answering this question with only this data would be valid. These G-rated movies, though a small number, might have really different budgets or have low budget but super high revenue or vice versa. Since the diagnostic plots for both models do not look concerning, I think the issue with the model might have to do with some other issue in the data. 

# Question 4: Same Data, Different Goals
Answering for Question 1
a) Inference: the population could be movies that were released within the interval of years that this dataset possesses, and for those movies that the data for budget, domestic gross revenue, and whether it passes the Bechdel test are available to put into the model. I did exclude 18 observations from the data because they were missing data for domestic gross revenue. It is also important to note that movies that have not posted their financial information would not be able to be represented in this model, and this occurrence might be more prevalent among certain types of movies, perhaps those that didn't perform as well. For assumptions, I would check for independence (the financial success of the first movie in the series might increase the budget of the sequel), as well as the normality of residuals (I remember the data looked a little skewed before log-transforming). And like earlier, I would check for really extreme outliers.

b) Prediction: Ideally, the prediction would be made before the movie is released, but there is the issue of obtaining whether a movie passes the Bechdel test or not. We would either have to wait until the movie is released to watch it, but not look at the revenue, or be able to access the Bechdel test result after the movie is finished but before its release. Hopefully movie budget would be available but I am not sure when that data gets released, similarly with the Bechdel test. I would still use a linear regression model because we are looking at continuous outcomes. To measure how well the model predicts, I would do cross-validation to estimate prediction error, so we can look at the RMSE, Rsquared, and the MAE from that cross validation output. 
I would report the following:
- variables we used in the model (budget, domestic gross revenue, Bechdel test results)
- the coefficients and p values we received in the model output
- procedure for cross validation (how many folds we used to train and test the model)
- values for RMSE, MAE, and Rsquared
- general conclusions on the fit and prediction accuracy of the model
